The Inimitable Quran Project. Synthetic English narration of a research draft. This is a spoken adaptation of the English discussion, not Quranic recitation. Arabic quotations are presented in English, and tables are explained in prose.

The Head Ablaze.

An old man is praying. Before he asks for what he needs, he describes what age has done to him. His strength is failing. His hair has whitened. Yet the sentence in which he speaks does something more particular than report those facts:

An image-preserving translation is: “And the head has blazed with gray hair.” The Arabic is the middle clause of Quran chapter 19, verse 4. 

The expression is unfamiliar enough in English to invite a second look. A head does not ordinarily blaze with grayness. Why describe aging through fire? Why make the head, rather than the hair, the subject? And what does this image contribute to a prayer?

These questions can be investigated before deciding whether the Quran is revelation. We need not pretend that the theological question is unimportant. It is the larger question of this book. But a reader should be able to inspect the evidence offered in its support. Calling a sentence miraculous cannot replace explaining how it works.

This chapter therefore begins with a small, examinable claim: the relationship between the grammar and the image contributes to a recognizable literary effect. Whether that effect is admirable is a further judgment. Whether it belongs to a sustained achievement beyond human productive capacity is further still.

A sentence inside a prayer.

The speaker is Zakariya, or Zechariah. Chapter 19, verses 2 through 3 introduce the account as a remembrance of divine mercy and describe his private calling upon his Lord. Verse 4 gives his words. In verses 5 through 6 he expresses concern about those who will follow him, describes his wife as unable to bear children, and asks for a successor who will inherit and be pleasing to God. The precise character of the inheritance is an exegetical question; nothing in the present argument requires settling it. 

Here is an English rendering of verse 4:

He said: “My Lord, my bones have weakened, and the head has blazed with gray hair. In calling upon You, my Lord, I have never been wretched.”

This working translation preserves the fire image while making one grammatical accommodation: Arabic has the singular al azm, “the bone,” where the translation uses “my bones.” Its final sentence deliberately stays close to the wording; the familiar sense of not having been disappointed in prayer is an interpretation supported by al Tabari’s commentary.
The verse can be read as moving from diminished bodily strength to visible aging and then to remembered confidence in God. That is the reading developed here, not a diagram supplied by the text. It has a basis readers can check: the order of the clauses, the physical descriptions, and the final statement about prayer. The apparent obstacle to Zakariya’s request and his reason for making it are brought together.

What the grammar lets us see.

The central clause has three written words. That count uses the ordinary spacing of the Arabic, including the prefixed conjunction within the first word; it is not a claim about a uniquely correct linguistic tokenization.

Consider the three elements. First, "and blazed": a conjunction plus a past-tense verb, picturing a happening through ignition or blazing. Second, "the head": a nominative noun and the grammatical subject of the verb. The head is the thing of which blazing is predicated. Third, "grayness," or "gray hair": an accusative indefinite noun, identifying the respect in which the head has blazed.

The case and verb information can be checked in the Quranic Arabic Corpus. The interpretation of the last word as a specifying accusative, tamyeez, follows the grammatical analysis developed in the classical discussion below. The Corpus’s word-by-word page identifies its accusative case; that fact alone is not a complete analysis of its syntactic function. 

On the tamyeez analysis, grayness specifies an otherwise surprising attribution: the head has blazed, in respect of gray hair. It is not an object that the head burns. Nor is “head” an agent deliberately performing an action. “Grammatical subject” describes its role in the sentence, not a claim about intention or physical causation.

This distinction matters because loose explanations can turn an intelligible construction into a false mystery. Arabic is not violating its grammar here. It is using a grammatical possibility to present a relationship in a particular way.

Al Tabari also preserves a useful complication. He reports disagreement over the accusative shayban: one analysis takes it as a verbal noun expressing the sense of becoming gray; another treats it as specification or explanation. The existence of this disagreement does not remove the head’s grammatical role. It does prevent us from presenting one account of the final accusative as the only analysis ever available. 

Al Jurjani’s invitation to compare.

The attribution of this example to Abd al Qahir al Jurjani can be made precise. In Dalail al Ijaz, paragraphs 91 through 93 of Mahmud Muhammad Shakir’s edition, he argues that naming the metaphor does not adequately explain the expression’s merit. The construction matters: the verb is attributed to the head, with grayness following in specification. He contrasts this with formulations making gray hair the subject and explains the Quranic construction through the idea of pervasive spread. He also discusses the definite expression “the head,” whose possessor is understood from context. The passage is on printed pages 100 through 102 of the third edition, fourteen thirteen in the Islamic calendar, or nineteen ninety-two. These pages and the edition statement have been checked against scanned images. 

His procedure gives the reader work to do. Keep something constant, alter something else, and inspect the consequence. It is a way to make a literary explanation answerable to the wording.

The following comparisons are analytical alternatives, not Quranic text. The two alternatives follow the constructions considered by al-Jurjani and are given here in English. The plain statement is a teaching paraphrase.

Compare three versions. The plain paraphrase, "My hair has turned gray," states the condition without the fire image. Alternative A, "The gray hair of the head blazed," makes gray hair the grammatical subject. Alternative B, "Gray hair blazed in the head," presents the head as the location.

The instructional advantage is also the limitation. We can see that the alternatives organize attention differently. We cannot infer that the less vivid English paraphrase represents the best humanity can compose. A demonstration designed to isolate a feature is not a literary championship.

Nor should “pervasive spread” become an anatomical measurement. The expression presents aging through an encompassing image; it does not give a percentage of white hairs. A reader might accept the larger impression while declining to infer that literally every hair has whitened. The distinction keeps literary interpretation proportionate to what language can establish.

Why the image belongs here.

Consider an objection that a sympathetic reading should not brush aside: fire is energetic, whereas old age is associated with loss of energy. Might “blazing” be an extravagant or even ill-chosen image?

It would be ill-chosen if the clause required every property of fire to apply to an aging man. But a metaphor selects a relationship. Brightness, spread, and the change in appearance can matter without implying youthful vigor. Ibn Ashur develops the image through a shining appearance spreading across a dark surface. He also reads the physical descriptions as an appeal for mercy rather than information God needs to learn. 

That last observation helps recover the sentence’s purpose. Zakariya is addressing the one to whom his condition is already known. The language presents his need within a relationship. One need not share the prayer’s theology to recognize this as its communicative situation.

On the reading offered here, the clause’s vigor makes the advance of age vivid. The loss of strength does not prevent the description from having force. Indeed, the contrast may intensify the presentation: the speaker is weakening while the visible signs of age seem active. This is an interpretive proposal. It should be tested against the surrounding passage, not presented as a hidden physical fact or a measured psychological effect.

There is also a difference between seeing and being told. “I am old” supplies a category. A description of weakness and whitened hair gives the reader particulars through which to imagine the predicament. The subsequent statement of confidence prevents the verse from ending with bodily decline. The prayer continues beyond what the body appears to permit.

This reading offers a reason to value the image besides its novelty. It contributes to the speaker’s position and the request that follows. If we removed it, the prayer would still contain aging and need, but one of its ways of making them present would disappear. That is a defensible account of contribution. It is not proof that no alternative could contribute equally well by different means.

The modern study of classical poetics can sharpen this distinction. Lara Harb’s publisher-provided summary of her chapter on nazm describes sentence construction as capable of prompting discovery through implicit meaning and context. It situates Quranic and poetic beauty within a connected field of analysis. This is a useful research orientation, not an empirical finding about how every reader experiences chapter 19, verse 4. Only the chapter summary and bibliographic information were inspected for this draft. 

Give the alternative explanation its strength.

A skeptical reader may accept the entire interpretation and still say: this is what accomplished literature does. It makes grammar, imagery, and situation work together. Why should this example count against exceptional human authorship?

At this stage it does not decide between the explanations. A striking and well-integrated metaphor is compatible with human literary skill. It would be circular to define the effect as superhuman because it occurs in scripture and then use the effect to prove that the scripture is superhuman.

The fair response is to enlarge the investigation. Examine accomplished Arabic writing in context, including writing whose effects differ from the Quran’s. Give each passage an opportunity to succeed at its own purpose. A restrained account of aging may be excellent because it withholds the dramatic image this verse supplies. A poem may develop an image over many lines because its purpose differs from the compression of a prayer.

A comparison therefore needs two questions. How effectively does each work accomplish its purpose? And, where the purposes genuinely overlap, which differences in expression matter? Neither question is answered by counting metaphors or by penalizing another work for lacking the Quran’s exact features.

The strongest human-authorship account can accommodate exceptional achievement. It need not predict ordinary language, obvious flaws, or unevenness in every short passage. To challenge that account, later chapters must investigate sustained performance, complete compositions, historical evidence, and fair alternatives. Even then, literary conclusions and conclusions about origin require separate reasoning.

There is an equally important challenge to the favorable interpretation itself. Perhaps the sense of comprehensive grayness arises mainly from our prior knowledge that the speaker is old. Perhaps familiarity makes the original seem inevitable. Perhaps an unfamiliar reader would regard a different construction as clearer. These possibilities do not refute al Jurjani’s analysis in advance. They identify what an investigation would have to distinguish.

What measurement could add.

The comparison can generate researchable questions without turning interpretation into a fictitious score. One proposed study would ask proficient Arabic readers to judge several carefully reviewed versions of the sentence. It would separate at least two tasks: an inference about how extensive the grayness appears, and a judgment of how well the wording serves the prayer. The first asks about communicated meaning; the second asks about literary fitness.

A simple descriptive contrast would be:

The difference in perceived extent equals the average rating of the original, minus the average rating of the alternative.

Here, each average would summarize readers’ ratings of perceived extent under a predefined scale, provided that treating its intervals as comparable is justified. Otherwise, the analysis should report ordered-category probabilities or paired preference proportions. A positive difference would mean that these readers, under these conditions, judged the original to suggest more pervasive grayness. It would not measure the percentage of an actual head that had whitened, and it would not establish divine authorship.

No such study has been conducted for this chapter. This calculation specifies a possible observation; it reports no result.

To make the study informative, the versions would need grammatical review, randomized presentation, and controls drawn from accomplished human writing. Some alternatives should be intended as improvements. Recognition and prior familiarity must be recorded, since simply hiding the source label cannot make a famous verse anonymous. Presenting the clause alone and within its prayer would help investigate the contribution of context, although the precise design must avoid teaching participants the contrast before measuring it.

Readers may disagree systematically. Specialists might distinguish a construction that other readers scarcely notice. Religious commitment might correlate with judgments, or it might not. The data should show those possibilities instead of averaging them away. Repeated judgments from one person and repeated versions of one sentence cannot be treated as independent witnesses to a universal claim.

One especially useful outcome would be a division between interpretation and preference. Readers might agree that the original presents more comprehensive grayness while differing over whether that is desirable. Such a result would strengthen a linguistic account while leaving an aesthetic dispute open. Conversely, if context eliminates the difference between constructions, that would narrow the claim we should make for the grammar alone.

The evidence we can carry forward.

The example now yields something more definite than an invitation to admire Arabic. Its wording is available for inspection. The head is the grammatical subject of blazing. An established classical interpretation explains the final accusative as specifying grayness and connects the construction with pervasive spread. The original attribution to al Jurjani is verifiable. A reading of the whole verse relates its physical imagery to need, remembered confidence, and prayer.

These findings occupy different levels. The grammatical forms are observations. The account of their effect is an interpretation. Calling that effect well suited to the prayer is a judgment. An argument that revelation best explains the Quran’s achievement would have to incorporate this evidence alongside much more, including evidence that could count against it.

The affirmative case gains credibility when those levels remain visible. It can invite the reader to recognize an achievement without demanding an immediate verdict on origin. It can also learn from a reader who accepts the grammatical analysis but disputes the evaluation.

We have examined one clause within one prayer. The next step is to examine a complete composition, where individual choices must contribute to a whole. The relevant question will become harder and more useful: how do the parts work together, and what would a serious comparison have to preserve?

End of this chapter. Sources, Arabic passages, and research notes are available in the written edition.
